reason: The original converse incorrectly invoked order \(p-1\) for \(-a\), although only order \((p-1)/2\) was assumed. The repaired argument directly proves that every exponent annihilating \(a\) is divisible by \(p-1\).
text:
Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Since \(a^m\not\equiv1\pmod p\) but \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\), we have \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Therefore \(2m\mid2n\), so \(m\mid n\). Together with \((-a)^m\equiv1\), this proves \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Because \(m\) is odd,
\[
a^m=(-1)^m(-a)^m\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
while \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \((-a)^{2n}=a^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(m\mid2n\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\); write \(n=qm\). Then
\[
1\equiv a^n=(a^m)^q\equiv(-1)^q\pmod p.
\]
As \(p\) is odd, this forces \(q\) to be even. Thus \(2m\mid n\), and consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\). Therefore \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).
